Unsupervised Conformal Inference: Bootstrapping and Alignment to Control LLM Uncertainty

Lingyou Pang ††thanks: Correspondence: lyopang@ucdavis.edu Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of California, Davis     Lei Huang Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of California, Davis     Jianyu Lin Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Johns Hopkins University     Tianyu Wang Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Johns Hopkins University     Akira Horiguchi Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of California, Davis     Alexander Aue ††thanks: These authors jointly supervised this work. Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of California, Davis     Carey E. Priebe††footnotemark: Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, Johns Hopkins University
Abstract

Deploying black-box LLMs requires managing uncertainty in the absence of token-level probability or true labels. We propose introducing an unsupervised conformal inference framework for generation, which integrates: generative models, incorporating: (i) an LLM-compatible atypical score derived from response-embedding Gram matrix, (ii) UCP combined with a bootstrapping variant (BB-UCP) that aggregates residuals to refine quantile precision while maintaining distribution-free, finite-sample coverage, and (iii) conformal alignment, which calibrates a single strictness parameter τ\tau so a user predicate (e.g., factuality lift) holds on unseen batches with probability ≥1−α\geq 1-\alpha. Across different benchmark datasets, our gates achieve close-to-nominal coverage and provide tighter, more stable thresholds than split UCP, while consistently reducing the severity of hallucination, outperforming lightweight per-response detectors with similar computational demands. The result is a label-free, API-compatible gate for test-time filtering that turns geometric signals into calibrated, goal-aligned decisions.

1 Introduction

Reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models (LLMs) is needed for trustworthy AI. An assertive yet baseless claim can swiftly spread and cause damage, but for most practitioners, frontier models arrive only as black-box APIs with no access to gradients, exact log probabilities, or hidden states [18]. Hence deployment teams must make keep-or-discard decisions from samples alone.

In black-box deployments, LLM uncertainty must be inferred from the sampled outputs themselves. Query-only signals include: (i) semantic-entropy methods that quantify dispersion across equivalence classes of responses and are effective for hallucination detection [8, 11]; (ii) self-consistency, which uses agreement among independently sampled answers as a proxy for confidence [31, 30]; and (iii) geometry-based measures computed from response embeddings—e.g., local density or Gram-volume statistics—that correlate with quality and robustness [22, 17]. Because these signals require neither logits nor gradients, they are natural conformity scores for our unsupervised conformal calibration; in parallel, conformal wrappers for language modeling and factuality control are emerging [23, 20].

Conformal prediction (CP) is model-agnostic and supplies finite-sample, distribution-free guarantees [2, 29]. However, the generative workflow breaks the classical supervised setting: prompts are not quantifiable covariates. A practical procedure must therefore calibrate in a label-only regime and use few, parallelizable API calls to expensive models.

We introduce a practical unsupervised conformal prediction (UCP) framework that increases data efficiency, reduces computation via bootstrapped conformal calibration, and reconciles heterogeneous modalities through conformal alignment, while delivering distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees and strong empirical gains in hallucination detection and factuality. Our framework calibrates directly on raw outputs and is compatible with black-box APIs:

  1. 1.

    an LLM-friendly atypicality score based on inner-product interaction energy of the response-embedding Gram matrix (unit-norm, cosine), yielding a bounded, exchangeability-compatible conformity score;

  2. 2.

    batched unsupervised conformal procedures—split UCP for single-batch queries and new batched variants (B-UCP and bootstrap-stabilized BB-UCP )—with finite-sample coverage under batch exchangeability and improved stability/efficiency over split UCP;

  3. 3.

    conformal alignment: a batch-level calibration of a single strictness knob τ\tau that ensures any predicate (e.g., factuality improvement) holds on unseen batches with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, enabling label-free test-time gating

The structure of the paper is outlined as follows. §2 explores query-only UQ and the foundational unsupervised CP techniques. In §3, we introduce the concepts of Gram-matrix typicality, batched/bootstrapped calibration, and conformal alignment. Experimental outcomes are presented in §4, while §5 discusses conclusions and future research directions.

2 Background

2.1 Conformal Prediction for Generative Outputs

Conformal prediction (CP) is a model-agnostic, distribution-free method that turns arbitrary scores into set-valued inferences with finite-sample guarantees under a common exchangeability assumption [28, 2, 16]. Classical assumptions can be relaxed via covariate-shift and dependence-aware extensions [4, 9]. Conformal Risk Control [3] not only addresses coverage but also aims to manage expected losses. Recent developments in language models use conformal calibration to enhance modeling accuracy, concentrating on removing and verifying claims [23, 20, 5].

Building on the concepts in [28, 16, 15, 25], we adopt the formal definitions of Full-UCP and Split-UCP as presented in Wasserman [32]. The corresponding algorithms also appear in the Appendix. We observe the responses Y1:nY_{1:n} paired with fixed prompts X1:nX_{1:n} and a future pair (Xn+1,Yn+1)(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1}). We primarily calibrate on the responses YY (i.e., model outputs), treating prompts/contexts XX as covariates that may be implicit. We treat Y1:nY_{1:n} as exchangeable. We define residuals via a permutation-invariant map ϕ\phi by Ri=ϕ⁡(Yi,𝒮i)R_{i}=\phi(Y_{i};\mathcal{S}_{i}). For tolerance α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), we target Pr⁡Yn+1∈Cn≥1−α\Pr{Y_{n+1}\in C_{n}}\geq 1-\alpha.

Full-UCP augments data with a candidate yn+1y_{n+1}, and residuals are recalculated for the augmented set {Y1,…,Yn,yn+1}\{Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n},y_{n+1}\}. A conformal pp-value is then derived from the residual ranking, incorporating yy when π⁡(y)≥α\pi(y)\geq\alpha. Split-UCP partitions the data into sets 𝒟1={Yi:i∈I1}\mathcal{D}_{1}=\{Y_{i}\colon i\in I_{1}\} and 𝒟2={Yi:i∈I2}\mathcal{D}_{2}=\{Y_{i}\colon i\in I_{2}\}, where index sets I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} partition the set {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}. We then calculate calibration residuals Ri=ϕ⁡(Yi,𝒟1)R_{i}=\phi(Y_{i};\mathcal{D}_{1}) for i∈I2i\in I_{2} to establish the (1−α)​(1+1|I2|)(1-\alpha)(1+\frac{1}{|I_{2}|})-quantile qq of these residual values, subsequently yielding the set Cn={y:ϕ⁡(y,𝒟1)≤q}C_{n}=\{y\colon\phi(y;\mathcal{D}_{1})\leq q\}. In addition, the Split-UCP marginal theorem states that under exchangeability of (Y1:n,Yn+1)(Y_{1:n},Y_{n+1}), the resulting set CnC_{n} satisfies Pr{Yn+1∈Cn}≥1−α\Pr\{Y_{n+1}\in C_{n}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

Full-UCP can be computationally inefficient due to retraining and ineffective searching over future candidates yy (grid/root-finding). On the other hand, Split-UCP is data-inefficient as only the calibration split 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2} influences the quantile, leading to sample-splitting costs. The challenges motivate us to design our framework for better alignment with the generative stochastic process P⁡(Y∣X)P(Y\mid X) to ensure that practical applications effectively capture underlying variability.

2.2 Gram Matrix Construction, Inner–Product Energy, and Atypical Score

To quantify LLM response uncertainty, we build our framework on the response-embedding Gram matrix. Given nn responses Y1,…,YnY_{1},\dots,Y_{n} with embeddings vi≔ψ⁡(Yi)∈ℝdv_{i}\coloneqq\psi(Y_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we stack the embeddings as rows to create the matrix V∈ℝn×dV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with Vi,:=vi⊤V_{i,:}=v_{i}^{\top} and form the (uncentered) Gram G≔V​V⊤∈ℝn×nG\coloneqq VV^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} with entries Gi​j=⟨vi,vj⟩G_{ij}=\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle, where unit–norm embeddings ‖vi‖2=1\|v_{i}\|_{2}=1 by default.

We then define the inner–product (interaction) energy:

e(i;G):=∥G:,i∥2=∥Vvi∥2.e(i;G)\;:=\;\|G_{:,i}\|_{2}\;=\;\|V\,v_{i}\|_{2}. (2.1)

In unit–norm embeddings, e⁡(i,G)=(∑j=1ncos2⁡θi​j)1/2e(i;G)=\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\cos^{2}\theta_{ij}\bigr)^{1/2}, where θi​j\theta_{ij} denotes the angle between viv_{i} and vjv_{j}. Thus, e​(i,G)2e(i;G)^{2} quantifies the total squared directional alignment of viv_{i} with its peers. Since cos2\cos^{2} treats aligned and anti-aligned directions equally, a large e⁡(i,G)e(i;G) indicates central, redundant elements (high agreement), while a small e⁡(i,G)e(i;G) denotes unique or irrelevant content (high novelty). The following theorem states that e⁡(⋅,G)e(\cdot;G) ranges from 11 to n\sqrt{n} (the proof is available in the Appendix).

Theorem 2.1 (Unit–norm interaction–energy bound).

If ‖vi‖2=1\|v_{i}\|_{2}=1 for all ii, then 1≤e⁡(i,G)≤n1\leq e(i;G)\leq\sqrt{n} for each ii. Equality e⁡(i,G)=ne(i;G)=\sqrt{n} holds when viv_{i} is perfectly aligned with all vjv_{j}; e⁡(i,G)=1e(i;G)=1 when viv_{i} is orthogonal to all vjv_{j} for j≠ij\neq i.

Letting BEB_{E} denote the supremum of e⁡(⋅,G)e(\cdot;G), we define the Atypical Score as

Φ⁡(i,G):= 1−e⁡(i,G)BE∈[0,1].\Phi(i;G)\;:=\;1-\frac{e(i;G)}{B_{E}}\;\in[0,1]. (2.2)

Under unit-norm embeddings, the upper bound BEB_{E} equals n\sqrt{n}. Note that any strictly monotone transform of ee is equivalent for ranking.

3 Methodology

3.1 Batch Unsupervised Conformal Prediction

We adapt UCP to a batched setting that gathers information across exchangeable batches and may stabilize calibration using a within-batch bootstrap. For notational simplicity, assume there are n+1=(J+1)​In+1=(J{+}1)I responses Y1,…,Yn+1Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n+1} for pre-chosen integers JJ and II. Partition the n+1n+1 responses into J+1J{+}1 disjoint batches ℬj={Yj,1,…,Yj,I}\mathcal{B}_{j}=\{Y_{j,1},\dots,Y_{j,I}\} for j=1,…,J+1j=1,\dots,J{+}1. The entire §3 assumes batch exchangeability, i.e., that the J+1J+1 batches ℬ1,…,ℬJ,ℬJ+1\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{J},\,\mathcal{B}_{J{+}1} are i.i.d. and that within each batch the responses are exchangeable. (The latter condition is also called partial exchangeability [7].) Thus we will assume without loss of generality that Yn+1=YJ+1,IY_{n+1}=Y_{J{+}1,I}.

We design two statistically distinct methods under this setting:

  • •

    Batch-UCP (B-UCP). For each calibration batch jj, residuals are computed within batches against leave-one-out Gram matrix base, where Rj,i=ϕ⁡(Yj,i,ℬj,−i)R_{j,i}=\phi(Y_{j,i};\mathcal{B}_{j,-i}) using a bounded, permutation-invariant score ϕ∈[0,Bϕ]\phi\!\in[0,B_{\phi}]. Pool {Rj,i}j=1:J,i=1:I\{R_{j,i}\}_{j=1{:}J,\;i=1{:}I} and take a single adjusted conformal quantile.

  • •

    Batch Bootstrap-UCP (BB-UCP). For each calibration batch jj, bootstrap the empirical residual multiset {Rj,i}i=1I\{R_{j,i}\}_{i=1}^{I} to obtain {Sj,k}k=1K\{S_{j,k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. Pool {Sj,k}j,k\{S_{j,k}\}_{j,k} and apply the same adjusted quantile. The bootstrap mitigates noise caused by irregularity from outlier batches, maintaining exchangeability.

The block below clarifies how B-UCP and BB-UCP differ. We present the formal algorithms in the Appendix (Algorithms B.3–B.4).

Under the batch exchangeability assumption, we have the following coverage guarantees, and we present the proofs in the Appendix.

Theorem 3.1 (B-UCP coverage).

The prediction set CnC_{n} returned by Batch U-CP satisfies Pr{Yn+1∈Cn}≥1−α.\Pr\{Y_{n+1}\in C_{n}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

Theorem 3.2 (BB-UCP coverage).

The prediction set CnC_{n} returned by Batch Bootstrap U-CP satisfies Pr{Yn+1∈Cn}≥1−α.\Pr\{Y_{n+1}\in C_{n}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

Our design incorporates three main mechanisms.

  1. 1)

    Batching. In the unsupervised setting, conventional CP loses the easy exchangeability of supervised CP because the conformity score depends on the other responses. By organizing data into exchangeable batches and using within-batch leave-one-out residuals (each Rj,iR_{j,i} computed against a base of size I−1I{-}1), we effectively re-enable cross-validation–style conformalization.

  2. 2)

    Within-batch LOO under batch exchangeability. This alignment makes the calibration and test residual laws match, removing the split-sample penalty in split-UCP (which inflates the order-statistic index) and yielding tighter thresholds at a fixed risk level.

  3. 3)

    Bootstrap aggregation. Averaging replicated empirical laws within each batch stabilizes the empirical quantile and down-weights idiosyncratic batches, reducing the chance of underestimating the target quantile. Realized coverage therefore tends to be slightly conservative while intervals remain short. Resampling {Rj,i}\{R_{j,i}\} is inexpensive and preserves exchangeability; and because the method is rank-based, any strictly non-decreasing transform of ϕ\phi leaves CnC_{n} unchanged. These effects anticipate our observations: BB-UCP is typically more conservative than split-UCP yet produces tighter, more stable intervals.

3.2 Conformal Alignment

Conformal alignment functions as a quality control technique across various modalities, enabling multilevel filtering and alignment superior to standard UCP schemes. Initially, we parameterize strictness using a single knob τ∈[0,1]\tau\!\in\![0,1] to filter batches with a low-cost, consistently available signal (here, the Gram matrix inner energy). During calibration, this signal is aligned with a rare or expensive quality measure (e.g., factuality), enabling deployment with just the low-cost signal while retaining the calibrated assurance Pr⁡(predicate on future batch)≥1−α\Pr(\text{predicate on future batch})\!\geq\!1-\alpha. The idea scales to various contexts: establishing an accessible, cost-effective score allows the use of the same method to determine a global τ^\hat{\tau} from past batches, which is then applied to unlabeled new data. By utilizing text and Gram scores, the predicate can adapt any non-decreasing, right-continuous batch metric to inexpensive scores derived from text, vision, audio, or multimodal embeddings, offering substantial flexibility and a wide range of applications.

Similar to §3.1, partition the data into JJ disjoint batches ℬj={Yj,1,…,Yj,I}\mathcal{B}_{j}=\{Y_{j,1},\dots,Y_{j,I}\} for j=1,…,Jj=1,\dots,J, with {ℬj}j=1J+1\{\mathcal{B}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J+1} exchangeable and ℬJ+1\mathcal{B}_{J+1} the future batch. Let ℛ​𝒞\mathcal{RC} be the space of right-continuous, non-decreasing maps [0,1]→[0,1][0,1]\!\to\![0,1], and define ψ:(𝒴I)→ℛ​𝒞\psi:\binom{\mathcal{Y}}{I}\!\to\!\mathcal{RC}. For each batch jj, set 𝒫j​(⋅)=ψ⁡(ℬj)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\cdot)=\psi(\mathcal{B}_{j}); then 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} is non-decreasing and right-continuous, and {𝒫j}\{\mathcal{P}_{j}\} is exchangeable.

We use 𝒫j​(τ)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\tau) as a batch predicate with a subset-selection parameter τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], which describes the jj-th batch. For instance, let J^j​(τ)⊆{1,…,I}\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau)\subseteq\{1,\dots,I\} be right-continuous filtered sets; that is, for any 0≤τ<τ′≤10\leq\tau<\tau^{\prime}\leq 1 there exists δ>0\delta>0 with J^j​(τ′)⊂J^j​(τ)=J^j​(τ+δ)\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau^{\prime})\subset\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau)=\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau+\delta). From the set J^j​(τ)\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau) of indices, we define 𝒫j​(τ)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\tau) as the indicator of the event “J^j​(τ)\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau) satisfies property A” where “property A” is to be determined according to a specific prediction target. We search for τ^\widehat{\tau} such that 𝒫J+1​(τ^)=1\mathcal{P}_{J+1}(\widehat{\tau})=1 with high probability, which means that the selected set J^J+1​(τ^)\widehat{J}_{J+1}(\hat{\tau}) satisfies “property A” with high probability.

Define the minimal passing strictness

Sj≔min⁡{τ∈[0,1]:𝒫j​(τ)=1}∈[0,1],S_{j}\coloneqq\min\{\tau\in[0,1]\colon\mathcal{P}_{j}(\tau)=1\}\in[0,1], (3.1)

with inf∅=1\inf\varnothing=1. Let K=⌈(1−α)​(J+1)⌉K=\lceil(1-\alpha)(J+1)\rceil and calibrate τ^\widehat{\tau} as the KK-th order statistic of {Sj}j=1J\{S_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J}.

A remark of Algorithm 3.1 is that, for a target threshold r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) which we want 𝒫J+1​(τ^)≥r\mathcal{P}_{J+1}(\hat{\tau})\geq r to hold for high probability, define 𝒫j′(τ)=𝟏{𝒫j(τ)≥r}\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{j}(\tau)=\mathbf{1}\{\mathcal{P}_{j}(\tau)\geq r\}. Then 𝒫j′\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{j} is also non-decreasing and right-continuous, and 𝒫j​(τ)≥r⇔𝒫j′​(τ)=1\mathcal{P}_{j}(\tau)\geq r\iff\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{j}(\tau)=1. Hence Algorithm 3.1 records {Sj′}\{S_{j}^{\prime}\} and returns a single τ^\widehat{\tau} with Pr{𝒫J+1(τ^)≥r}=Pr{𝒫J+1′(τ^)=1}≥1−α\Pr\{\mathcal{P}_{J+1}(\hat{\tau})\geq r\}=\Pr\{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}_{J+1}(\widehat{\tau})=1\}\geq 1-\alpha under exchangeability.

Theorem 3.3 (B-UCP alignment guarantee).

Assume the batches {Bj}j=1J+1\{B_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J+1} are exchangeable (which implies that predicates {𝒫j}j=1J+1\{\mathcal{P}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J+1} are exchangeable) and that each 𝒫j​(⋅)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\cdot) is non-decreasing and right-continuous in its argument τ\tau for j=1,…,J+1j=1,\dots,J{+}1. Then Algorithm 3.1 satisfies

Pr{𝒫J+1(τ^)=1}≥ 1−α.\Pr\!\left\{\ \mathcal{P}_{J+1}\bigl(\widehat{\tau}\bigr)=1\ \right\}\ \geq\ 1-\alpha.

By Theorem 3.3, any non-decreasing, right-continuous batch predicate calibrated across exchangeable batches yields a 1−α1-\alpha guarantee on the held-out batch. We now instantiate this scheme for black-box LLMs by selecting a cheap Gram-geometry self-consistency score QQ with the induced filter J^j​(τ)\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau) and a batch predicate 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} that encodes deployment goals (e.g., factuality lift), as specified next.

Let Qj,iQ_{j,i} denote the inner-product interaction energy e⁡(i,G)e(i;G) from Section 2.2 (unit-norm, cosine geometry). We keep high-consensus items via

J^j​(τ)≔{i:Qj,i>τ},\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau)\ \coloneqq\ \{\,i:\ Q_{j,i}>\tau\,\},

so larger τ\tau filters out more responses.

Let sj,i∈[0,1]s_{j,i}\!\in\![0,1] be a batch severity with larger = worse (e.g., factuality severity). In strictness τ\tau, set Kj​(τ)={i:Qj,i>τ}K_{j}(\tau)=\{i:Q_{j,i}>\tau\} and Dj​(τ)={i:Qj,i≤τ}D_{j}(\tau)=\{i:Q_{j,i}\leq\tau\}, and declare pass when the indicator is evaluated as 1, where

𝒫jCVAR(τ):={CVARq(sj,i:i∈Dj(τ))−CVARq(sj,i:i∈Kj(τ))⏟Δ​CVARj,τ​(q)≥δ}.\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{CVAR}}_{j}(\tau)\ :=\ \mathbf{1}\!\Big\{\underbrace{\mathrm{CVAR}_{q}(s_{j,i}:i\!\in\!D_{j}(\tau))-\mathrm{CVAR}_{q}(s_{j,i}:i\!\in\!K_{j}(\tau))}_{\Delta\mathrm{CVAR}_{j,\tau}(q)}\ \geq\ \delta\Big\}.

CVAR focuses on the worst tail. Requiring a positive gap means that the kept set reduces severe errors (rare but damaging hallucinations) relative to the dropped set [6, 35, 24, 1]. Because Kj​(τ)K_{j}(\tau) enlarges as τ\tau decreases, τ↦𝒫jCVAR​(τ)\tau\mapsto\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{CVAR}}_{j}(\tau) is non-decreasing/right-continuous, so Alg. 3.1 applies unchanged.

Let sj,is_{j,i} be a factuality severity in [0,1][0,1] (lower is better; e.g., BERTScore–F1 dissimilarity). The predicate 𝒫jF​(τ)=1\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{F}}_{j}(\tau)=1 asserts that the QQ-filtered subset attains a statistically significant median reduction in factuality severity (per the test above). Calibrating τ^\hat{\tau} across historical batches yields a single label-free gate which, using QQ alone at deployment, preserves this improvement on new batches with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha (Theorem 3.3). Applications include: (i) open-domain QA/RAG: ensure only consistent answers are shown; (ii) customer support and search snippets: reduce the risk of false confident statements; (iii) summarization/reporting: exclude sections that do not pass factual accuracy checks before publishing.

4 Experiments

We perform three experiments to study three research questions aligned with §3: (RQ1) within a single query, does BB-UCP produce tighter prediction sets than S-UCP at the same target miscoverage? (RQ2) across multiple queries, do B-/BB-UCP achieve nominal coverage and improve batch quality by discarding higher-severity responses? (RQ3) in cross-query alignment, can the calibrated global strictness τ^\hat{\tau} reliably yield batch-level severity reduction while preserving the conformal guarantee?

4.1 Experimental setup

We evaluate across four complementary QA datasets, each exhibiting a distinct failure mode: ASQA—ambiguity and underspecification [26]; NQ-Open—single-hop factoid retrieval [14, 13]; HotpotQA—multi-hop composition [33]; and AmbigQA—aliases and answer sets [19]. To probe sensitivity, we add two ablations: a decoding-entropy stress test and a vendor/model swap. For each open-domain QA prompt, we (i) synthesize a diverse response set by mixing plain answers, lightly enforced canonical answers, and structured noise outliers. This controlled injection is standard for stress test hallucination detection and semantic dispersion UQ signals [12, 22] and allows us to probe robustness under realistic contamination. All texts are embedded with a lightweight sentence encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). We stack unit-normalized embedding vectors by rows to form VV and then the Gram matrix G=V​V⊤G=VV^{\top}; (ii) expand the reference set with concise paraphrases to reduce aliasing; and (iii) characterize each candidate using a distance-based metric, Factuality Severity (FS). All artifacts are logged and kept provider-agnostic across OpenAI, Together, and Gemini [21, 10, 27].

We quantify answer quality with respect to references using BERTScore–F1 with baseline rescaling (roberta-large) [34] on the answer head (first sentence or a Final: field, truncated to ≤16\leq 16 tokens). Letting head⁡(a)\mathrm{head}(a) be the head of answer aa and ℛq\mathcal{R}_{q} the reference set, we define the severity

FS⁡(a)≔ 1−maxr∈ℛq⁡BERTScoreF1⁡(head⁡(a),r)∈[0,1],\mathrm{FS}(a)\ \coloneqq\ 1-\max_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{q}}\,\mathrm{BERTScoreF1}\!\big(\mathrm{head}(a),\,r\big)\ \in[0,1], (4.1)

so that a value of 00 indicates a near-paraphrase of some reference (high factual alignment), and a value near 11 flags semantic deviation. Scoring the head avoids rationale contamination and normalizes across style/length.

Given a batch BB and the kept subset K⁡(τ)K(\tau) after filtering by QQ, we summarize factuality lifting by the median reduction

ΔFS (τ)=median{FS(y):y∈B}−median{FS(y):y∈K(τ)}\Delta_{\text{FS }}(\tau)=\mathrm{median}\{FS(y):y\in B\}-\mathrm{median}\{FS(y):y\in K(\tau)\}

(larger is better). All conformal calibrations use the Gram inner–energy score ee from §3 and are implemented exactly as specified (S-/B-/BB-UCP and alignment). We fix random seeds, cache embeddings/Grams, and run identical pipelines on all datasets.

4.2 Experiment I — Single-Query Conformal Calibration (S-UCP vs. BB-UCP)

In the single-query regime, for each question qq we embed all candidate responses, form the unit-norm response Gram matrix GG, and compute the inner-product energy score QQ for each response. We then construct residuals within the same pool and repeatedly split into calibration/test subsets of fixed sizes. Split UCP thresholds test residuals by directly taking a quantile of residuals; BB-UCP additionally bootstraps the calibration residuals within the batch and aggregates the quantiles to stabilize the threshold. We report (i) empirical coverage against the 1−α1-\alpha target and (ii) an efficiency proxy given by the accepted sublevel endpoint q1−αq_{1-\alpha} (smaller is better).

Across AmbigQA, AmbigQA-ENT, ASQA, and HotpotQA, both S-UCP and BB-UCP achieve near-nominal coverage, while BB-UCP consistently achieves more conservative empirical coverage across repetitions and α\alpha and yields shorter interval length; see Fig. 1 (top/bottom). On NQ-Open and NQ-Open-Vend, performance is weaker: the answer pools are small and low-diversity, often collapsing into a single high-consensus “heap.” This compresses dispersion in Gram space, produces near-tied residual ranks, and blunts the bootstrap’s advantage; Split UCP ’s coverage remains close to target. Slightly enlarging pool size or boosting response diversity effectively restores similar qualitative improvements as seen in other datasets.

4.3 Experiment II — Cross-Query Calibration (BB-UCP) and Factuality Lifting

To mimic real-world deployment, each response set of the same query forms a batch. We run leave-one-query-out (LOQO) cross-validation: hold one batch for testing and calibrate on the rest. For every calibration batch we compute residuals from QQ under within-batch LOO, bootstrap residuals per batch, pool the bootstrapped (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantiles into a single threshold q1−αBBq^{\mathrm{BB}}_{1-\alpha}, and apply that global threshold to the held-out batch. We evaluate (i) empirical coverage vs. 1−α1-\alpha and (ii) factuality lifting via the median reduction in factuality severity, Δ​FS\Delta\mathrm{FS} (excluded minus kept; better positivity indicates improved prevention of hallucinations.).

LOQO empirical coverage closely tracks 1−α1-\alpha across risk levels and datasets (Fig. 2, top), demonstrating that a BB-UCP global threshold learned from historical queries generalizes to unseen queries. More importantly for deployment, filtering by q1−αBBq^{\mathrm{BB}}_{1-\alpha} consistently improves batch quality: Δ​FS>0\Delta\mathrm{FS}>0 across all datasets and all α\alpha (Fig. 2, bottom; The hardest panels are instructive: on NQ-Open, median Δ​FS≈0.209\Delta\mathrm{FS}\!\approx\!0.209 (largest among benchmarks) despite average empirical coverage falling short of the 95%95\% target (88.98% vs. 95.00%); NQ-Open-Vend shows the same trade-off (median Δ​FS≈0.112\Delta\mathrm{FS}\!\approx\!0.112, 92.88% vs. 95.00%) (Appendix C, Table 4). This under-coverage is attributable to small-NN/low-entropy pools that yield discretization effects and near-ties in residual ranks. As in Experiment I, standard operational tweaks—increasing per-query pool size or adding response diversity—tighten coverage without erasing the observed factuality lift.

4.4 Experiment III — Cross-Query Conformal Alignment (CVaR-gap)

We perform LOQO folds for conformal alignment as well. In each fold, for every calibration batch jj we scan a strictness grid τ\tau and evaluate the CVaR-gap predicate 𝒫jCVAR​(τ)\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{CVAR}}_{j}(\tau) at tail level qq and margin δ\delta, then record the minimal passing strictness SjS_{j}. We conformally calibrate a global τ^\hat{\tau} as the split-batch (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of {Sj}\{S_{j}\} (Alg. 3.1), then deploy on the held-out batch using only the cheap score QQ: keep K⁡(τ^)={i:Qi>τ^}K(\hat{\tau})=\{i:Q_{i}>\hat{\tau}\} and report (i) empirical pass rate against 1−α1-\alpha and (ii) factuality improvement via Δ​CVAR​(τ^)\Delta\mathrm{CVAR}(\hat{\tau}). Full predicate and implementation details are in Appendix B.5/C.

Alignment preserves the statistical target while delivering consistent factuality gains: for every dataset and every risk level, the reduction in factuality severity on the kept set is positive on average (Fig. 3). Notably, the largest median and mean improvements occur on the two hardest datasets—NQ-Open and NQ-Open-Vend—with median Δ​FS≈0.206\Delta\mathrm{FS}\!\approx\!0.206 and ≈0.112\approx\!0.112, respectively (Appendix C, Table 5). Aligning the affordable Gram-geometry score with the factuality signal provides an effective, economical filtering method, ensuring conformal assurance for new batches.

5 Conclusion

We introduced an unsupervised conformal inference framework for black-box LLMs that operates entirely on sampled outputs. The framework comprises three deployable components: (i) a Gram-geometry atypicality score based on unit-norm response-embedding inner products, yielding a bounded, interpretable, and stable signal; (ii) batched conformal procedures (B-UCP and the bootstrap-stabilized BB-UCP) that provide distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees under batch exchangeability while improving quantile stability and data efficiency over split UCP; and (iii) conformal alignment, which calibrates a global strictness parameter τ^\hat{\tau} so that a batch predicate (e.g., a CVaR-gap factuality lift) holds on new batches with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. Conformal alignment provides a principled way to synchronize an expensive signal (ground truth) with a cheaper proxy and performs well when deployment relies only on the proxy, yielding a probabilistic approach to multimodal signal gating and filtering.

Limitations and outlook.

Our guarantees assume exchangeability across batches and within-batch permutation invariance; violations due to drift or covariate shift motivate weighted or covariate-aware variants. Performance depends on embedding quality and normalization, underscoring the need for robustness audits and principled model/embedding selection. Predicate design (e.g., CVaR vs. median lifts and multi-metric trade-offs) invites cost-aware utilities and multi-task calibration. Extending alignment to multimodal settings and adding adaptive or online recalibration are promising directions for stronger reliability under non-stationarity.

Use of AI for language editing.

Proof.

Pr(Yn+1∈Cn)=Pr(ϕ(Yn+1,ℬJ+1,−I)≤q)=1−𝔼[𝟏{ϕ(Yn+1,ℬJ+1,−I)>q}].\Pr\bigl(Y_{n+1}\in C_{n}\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(\phi(Y_{n+1},\mathcal{B}_{J+1,-I})\leq q\bigr)=1-\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(Y_{n+1},\mathcal{B}_{J+1,-I})>q\}\bigr].

Also do virtual bootstrap in the future batch ℬJ+1\mathcal{B}_{J+1} to get {SJ+1,k}k=1K\{S_{J+1,k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. Independence across jj and identical distributions imply

𝔼[𝟏{ϕ(Yn+1,ℬJ+1,−I)>q}]=𝔼[1K∑k=1K𝟏{SJ+1,k>q}].\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(Y_{n+1},\mathcal{B}_{J+1,-I})>q\}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{S_{J+1,k}>q\}\right].

Let

λ^′:=inf{λ:1(J+1)​K∑j=1J+1∑k=1K𝟏{Sj,k>λ}≤α}\hat{\lambda}^{\prime}:=\inf\!\left\{\lambda:\frac{1}{(J+1)K}\sum_{j=1}^{J+1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{S_{j,k}>\lambda\}\leq\alpha\right\}
λ^:=Bϕ∧inf{λ:1(J+1)​K∑j=1J∑k=1K𝟏{Sj,k>λ}+1J+1≤α}.\hat{\lambda}:=B_{\phi}\wedge\inf\!\left\{\lambda:\frac{1}{(J+1)K}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{S_{j,k}>\lambda\}+\frac{1}{J+1}\leq\alpha\right\}.

Then λ^′≤λ^≤q\hat{\lambda}^{\prime}\leq\hat{\lambda}\leq q and the same exchangeability argument yields

𝔼[𝟏{ϕ(Yn+1,ℬJ+1,−I)>q}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{\phi(Y_{n+1},\mathcal{B}_{J+1,-I})>q\}\bigr] =𝔼[1K∑k=1K𝟏{SJ+1,k>q}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{S_{J+1,k}>q\}\right]
≤𝔼[1K∑k=1K𝟏{SJ+1,k>λ^′}]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{S_{J+1,k}>\hat{\lambda}^{\prime}\}\right]
=𝔼[1(J+1)​K∑j=1J+1∑k=1K𝟏{Sj,k>λ^′}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{(J+1)K}\sum_{j=1}^{J+1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{S_{j,k}>\hat{\lambda}^{\prime}\}\right]
≤α,\displaystyle\leq\alpha,

hence Pr⁡(Yn+1∈Cn)≥1−α\Pr(Y_{n+1}\in C_{n})\geq 1-\alpha. ∎

Remark.

The proof skills for Theorem 3.1 and 3.2 comes from the attempt to go back from conformal risk control to conformal prediction. In the proof we constructed a proper loss function to achieve this with a standard argument of CRC. This technique can be transfer to many other settings where we need to go back to CP from CRC.

B.4 Algorithmic details for the CVaR-gap predicate

Let Qj,iQ_{j,i} denote the inner-product interaction energy from Section 2.2 (unit-norm, cosine geometry). We keep high-consensus items via

J^j​(τ):={i:Qj,i>τ},\widehat{J}_{j}(\tau)\ :=\ \{\,i:\ Q_{j,i}>\tau\,\},

so larger τ\tau retains fewer and more self-consistent responses.

Let sj,i∈[0,1]s_{j,i}\!\in\![0,1] be a batch severity with larger = worse (e.g., factuality severity). At strictness τ\tau, define the kept and dropped sets Kj​(τ)={i:Qj,i>τ}K_{j}(\tau)=\{i:Q_{j,i}>\tau\} and Dj​(τ)={i:Qj,i≤τ}D_{j}(\tau)=\{i:Q_{j,i}\leq\tau\}. For a random variable XX with CDF FXF_{X}, the upper-tail Conditional Value-at-Risk at level q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) is

CVARq​(X):=11−q​∫q1VaRu​(X)​𝑑u,where​VaRu​(X)=inf{x:FX​(x)≥u}.\mathrm{CVAR}_{q}(X)\ :=\ \frac{1}{1-q}\int_{q}^{1}\mathrm{VaR}_{u}(X)\,du,\hskip 10.00002pt\text{where}\;\mathrm{VaR}_{u}(X)=\inf\{x:\,F_{X}(x)\geq u\}.

We instantiate a batch predicate that asks for a tail-risk improvement after filtering:

ΔCVARj,τ(q):=CVARq(sj,i:i∈Dj(τ))−CVARq(sj,i:i∈Kj(τ)),\Delta\mathrm{CVAR}_{j,\tau}(q)\ :=\ \mathrm{CVAR}_{q}\!\big(s_{j,i}:i\in D_{j}(\tau)\big)\;-\;\mathrm{CVAR}_{q}\!\big(s_{j,i}:i\in K_{j}(\tau)\big),
𝒫jCVAR(τ):= 1{ΔCVARj,τ(q)≥δ}.\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{CVAR}}_{j}(\tau)\ :=\ \mathbf{1}\{\Delta\mathrm{CVAR}_{j,\tau}(q)\geq\delta\}.

CVAR, also known as Expected Shortfall, focuses on the worst tail and is coherent and robust to heavy tails; demanding a positive CVAR gap concentrates the kept set on reliably low-severity answers and suppresses rare but severe failures.

Let F​Sj,iFS_{j,i} be a factuality severity in [0,1][0,1] (lower is better; e.g., BERTScore–F1 dissimilarity). The predicate 𝒫jF​(τ)=1\mathcal{P}^{\mathrm{F}}_{j}(\tau)=1 asserts that the QQ-filtered subset achieves a statistically significant median reduction in factuality severity (per the test above). Calibrating τ^\hat{\tau} across historical batches yields a single label-free gate which, when applied with QQ alone, preserves this improvement on new batches with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha (Theorem 3.3).

Appendix C Experiment

C.1 Appendix: Hallucination Experiment Settings and Configurations

For each question we generate a response set, compute Factuality Severity =1−maxr∈refs⁡BERTScore​-​F​1​(a,r)=1-\max_{r\in\text{refs}}\mathrm{BERTScore}\text{-}F1(a,r). All runs are seeded and logged to timestamped, self-describing CSVs: a per-answer file (scores, margins, types, decoding knobs) and a per-run file (dataset/split, sample counts, model/provider, seeds, thresholds, and paths). Together model IDs are normalized to serverless fallbacks to avoid availability regressions.

We evaluate across four core datasets—ASQA (dev), NQ-Open (validation), HotpotQA (validation), AmbigQA (dev)—plus two ablations that stress decoding entropy and vendor/model choice. Each configuration fixes decoding knobs and the normal/enforced/noise mix, while paraphrasing a canonical gold to reduce aliasing of surface forms.

Shared knobs: alias-normalization for Together; n_per_call=5; rate-limit ≈\approx 0.8s; severity mix weight logged; seeds: C1=42, C2=7, C3=11, C4=23, C5=23, C6=8.

We use minimal, auditable prompts. For paraphrasing the canonical gold: System: “You rewrite text. Output a succinct standalone paraphrase.” User: “Paraphrase the following answer in different wording, preserving the exact meaning and factual content. Keep it concise and standalone. Avoid hedging, qualifiers, or extra details. Answer: {gold}.” For normal answers: System: “Answer the question with the canonical short answer first; then add at most one brief justification. Be concise.” User: {question}. For enforced canonical answers: System: “Answer with the canonical short answer first; then a single, concrete supporting detail. Avoid aliasing, avoid hedging, avoid contradictory statements.” User: {question}. (Noise/outlier strings are programmatically injected: gibberish, off-topic, fabricated citations, prompt-injection strings, contradictions, emoji floods, and multilingual snippets.)

Embeddings: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with unit-norm rows; semantic-entropy uses a soft neighbor kernel above τ\tau (exponent κ=4\kappa{=}4) and a normalized −log-\log mapping to [0,1][0,1]. Severity-F1 uses bert-score with roberta-large (baseline-rescaled) on “answer heads” (first ≤\leq16 tokens) to limit verbosity bias. All artifacts are timestamped and saved as {dataset}_{model}_{stamp}__ns{N} for direct reuse in downstream risk control. This mirrors the same compute-aware calibration-to-deployment recipe we use for LLM-as-Judge.

C.2 More Results

Across Experiment 1, our methods perform strongly on the majority of benchmarks: on ASQA, HOTPOTQA, and both AMBIGQA panels (standard and entropy-ablation), Split-UCP consistently achieves nominal coverage while BB-UCP further tightens the coverage range and reduces variability—demonstrating the intended stability benefit of within-batch bagging under heterogeneous answer clouds with heavier tails. These results highlight two key strengths of our approach: (i) distribution-free coverage remains intact across diverse datasets, providers, and decoding knobs, and (ii) practical efficiency improves in harder settings, where bootstrapping stabilizes tail quantiles and yields shorter, more reliable acceptance regions at a fixed risk level.

NQ-OPEN and its variant NQ-OPEN-VEND show weakness due to small query pools and low-diversity factoids, leading to compressed Gram-space dispersion. This results in nearly tied residual ranks, reducing the visibility of BB-UCP’s advantage over Split-UCP.This behavior is an artifact of the small-NN/low-entropy regime rather than a failure of validity, and is readily mitigated in practice by slightly increasing the pool size or calibration-only diversity (or by modest geometry smoothing), after which these panels recover the same qualitative gains observed on ASQA, HOTPOTQA, and AMBIGQA.

Experiment 2

Experiment 2 shows that the factuality lift is not only consistent but strongest on the hardest panels. Aggregating the raw bars across all α\alpha values, the median Δ​FS\Delta\mathrm{FS} is strictly positive for every dataset (all panels, all α\alpha), confirming that the QQ-gate reliably reduces factuality severity on the kept set. Moreover, the largest median gains occur on NQ-OPEN and NQ-OPEN-VEND (aka EnqueueOpen/EnqueueOpenVend): NQ-OPEN achieves the top median improvement (Δ~​FS≈0.209\tilde{\Delta}\mathrm{FS}\!\approx\!0.209), with NQ-OPEN-VEND second (Δ~​FS≈0.112\tilde{\Delta}\mathrm{FS}\!\approx\!0.112), while the remaining benchmarks (ASQA, HOTPOTQA, AMBIGQA, AMBIGQA-ENT) are all positive as well. This “worst-case best” pattern indicates our gate concentrates probability mass on the most reliable answers precisely where the answer cloud is small and low-diversity. Coverage is slightly under nominal on average in those two hardest panels (mean gap ≈−6.0\approx\!-6.0 pp on NQ-OPEN; range of mean gaps across benchmarks ≈[−6.0,+0.8]\approx[-6.0,\,+0.8] pp), which is expected from small-NN discretization and near-tied ranks; it is also actionable—increasing the per-query pool or adding calibration-only diversity closes the shortfall without altering the factuality lift. Net: Experiment 2 provides a strong, data-backed claim of robustness (positive lift everywhere), effectiveness (largest gains on the hardest datasets), and practical tunability (coverage can be tightened by modest, standard knobs).
